strengths: Addresses an important problem: reliable pseudo-label selection for node classification under severe class imbalance. Recruiting existing unlabeled nodes avoids synthesizing node features and graph connections.

The evaluation is broad, covering five datasets, three GNN architectures, imbalance ratios up to 100, naturally imbalanced settings, and five repetitions with reported standard errors. Several reported improvements are substantial: on CiteSeer with GCN at ratio 10, F1 increases from the strongest baseline's 56.32 to 64.94.

The manuscript investigates minority-class pseudo-label errors and includes agreement diagnostics, ranking comparisons, component ablations, and sensitivity analyses. These investigations offer useful empirical insights beyond the final method's benchmark performance.

The appendix supplies dataset statistics, optimization settings, hyperparameter ranges, hardware details, and pseudocode. No material research ethics concern is apparent from the described benchmark experiments.
weaknesses: The contribution is insufficiently distinguished from its closest prior work. Section 6 describes M3S as filtering classifier pseudo-labels using clustering assignments, closely matching DPAM's central operation. The DPAM-plus-confidence ablation is relevant, but its relationship to M3S is not established, and an explicit matched comparison is missing. This makes it difficult to assess how much improvement comes from the proposed additions to existing self-training machinery.

Several supporting statistics are internally inconsistent. In Table 8, GCN at ratio 5 reports 11,593.60 aligned nodes and 2,308.40 discarded nodes, totaling 13,902 despite an unlabeled population of 13,632. These sets are defined as a partition. In Table 7, GCN at ratio 100 gives different standard errors for complementary set sizes, although their total is fixed. These discrepancies require corrected tables and per-run results; they weaken confidence in the evidence supporting DPAM.

The geometric filtering definition contains an unresolved inconsistency. Equation 5 measures distance to the assigned class center, but Equation 4 assigns labels through cluster centroids. An individual node's assigned center therefore need not be its nearest center, contrary to Section 4.3's assertion underlying the GI interpretation. The treatment of such nodes needs specification. Appendix C.6 also reverses the threshold's effect: increasing the rejection threshold makes filtering stricter.

The ablations provide mixed support for the necessity of the added components. In Table 11, geometric ranking alone achieves 75.85 versus 76.44 F1 for the full method on Cora, and 77.32 versus 77.38 on PubMed; these differences are small relative to the reported uncertainty. Adding DGIN lowers CiteSeer F1 from 58.71 to 57.51. Comparisons against fixed rank averaging and class-balanced or calibrated self-training would better establish the value of the particular RBO weighting and GI filter.

Reproducibility and computational practicality remain incompletely established. The manuscript provides no implementation link or selected configurations, does not define the F1 averaging convention, and leaves retraining initialization and updates to the unlabeled pool unclear. With 40–100 rounds and up to 2,000 training epochs per round, runtime and measured memory comparisons are needed to substantiate the practical advantage suggested by the discussion of baseline memory failures.

Some conclusions exceed the experimental evidence. Increasing the ratio from 20 to 50 or 100 also increases majority-class labels while retaining one minority label, so the trend does not isolate imbalance from annotation budget. Claims of consistent superiority also overlook results such as Computers-Random with GraphSAGE and Flickr balanced accuracy with GAT. Together with the unresolved reporting and comparison issues, these concerns outweigh the promising reported gains in the current submission.
